name: Network security / SIEM enrichment per-IP/per-asset rolling features
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Network security / SIEM enrichment with per-IP, per-asset and per-user rolling features for SOC detection rules and SIEM correlation
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A SOC / detection-engineering team computes per-IP, per-asset, per-user and per-(source × dest) rolling counters, velocities, distinct-port / distinct-host distributions, beaconing-interval distributions and impossible-travel distances on every network or auth event, and serves them in sub-millisecond reads to a SIEM correlation engine, a Sigma/Panther/Elastic detection rule, an XDR/UEBA scorer or a SOAR enrichment playbook so the rule fires in seconds rather than minutes.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Detect credential brute-force / password-spraying (MITRE T1110) by maintaining per-source-IP and per-account_id rolling counters of failed_logins, failure_ratio and n_unique(account_id) on 1m / 5m / 15m sliding windows, and firing when thresholds cross — without forcing the SIEM to re-scan raw events every minute. 2) Detect port-scan / horizontal-scan / network reconnaissance (T1046) by tracking n_unique(dest_port) and n_unique(dest_ip) per source IP in 60-second sliding windows (Cisco / Splunk Security Content rule shape). 3) Detect lateral movement (T1021 / T1570) by tracking per-asset velocity of new (source_host, dest_host, port) tuples, n_unique(dest_host) per source_host, and time-since-last-internal-RDP/SMB. 4) Detect C2 beaconing (T1071, T1095) by tracking per-(src_ip, dest_ip, dest_port) inter-arrival-time distribution / jitter (low standard deviation + consistent interval ≈ machine-driven beacon). 5) Enrich every event ingested into Splunk / Sentinel / Chronicle / Elastic with pre-computed per-IP/per-asset risk features so high-cardinality correlation rules don't blow up the SIEM's per-GB ingest cost and per-tenant search latency. 6) Power impossible-travel detection (per-user_id last_geo + last_ts vs current_geo + current_ts, distance / time_delta > airspeed threshold — Okta's 500 mph default).
domain_fit.event_shapes: auth_event {ts, src_ip, account_id, host, method (interactive/network/ssh/kerberos/ldap), success, reason, geo, asn, country, deployment}, flow_event {ts, src_ip, dest_ip, src_port, dest_port, proto, bytes_in, bytes_out, duration_ms, action (allowed/denied), vlan, asset_id}, dns_event {ts, src_ip, qname, qtype, rcode, response_ips, domain_age_d, ttl}, proxy_event {ts, src_ip, host, url, status, bytes_in, bytes_out, ua, ja3, ja4}, endpoint_event {ts, host_id, process, parent_process, cmdline, user, signed, file_hash}, vpn_event {ts, account_id, src_ip, geo, asn, success}. Volume is dominated by flow_event (NetFlow / VPC Flow Logs / Zeek conn.log) and proxy_event, with auth_event at much lower rate but high decision value. Dimensions: src_ip, dest_ip, src_port, dest_port, account_id, host_id / asset_id, geo, asn, country, proto, ja3/ja4 TLS fingerprint, parent/child process pair, and ordered tuples (src_ip × dest_port), (src_ip × dest_ip), (account_id × src_ip), (host_id × dest_host).
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of beava counters + n_unique (HLL) + velocity + distance + distribution / variance primitives in 1m / 5m / 15m / 1h / 24h sliding windows aligned to the de-facto detection-rule windows (Cisco / Splunk / Elastic / Sigma). Per-src_ip: count(failed_logins_5m), failure_ratio_5m, n_unique(account_id)_5m (password-spray signal), n_unique(dest_port)_60s (port-scan signal — Cisco PORT_THRESHOLD=20), n_unique(dest_ip)_60s (horizontal scan), velocity(connection_attempts_1m), distribution(country / ASN). Per-account_id: count(failed_logins_5m), n_unique(src_ip)_15m (distributed brute-force / 'low-and-slow' password spray), distance(last_geo, current_geo) / time_delta (impossible-travel — Microsoft windowed thresholds 500/1000/2000 miles × 2/4/6 h, Okta 500 mph). Per-host_id (asset): n_unique(dest_host_internal)_1h (lateral-movement signal), velocity(new_dest_host_pairs_5m), recency(last_internal_admin_protocol). Per-(src_ip × dest_ip × dest_port): inter-arrival-time mean, stddev, jitter (beaconing signal — low stddev + consistent interval implies C2 heartbeat at e.g. 60 s or 90 s). Per-dns: n_unique(qname_per_src_ip)_5m, ratio of NXDOMAIN responses (DGA signal). EWMA / Welford's online variance over per-(asset, signal) baselines feeds UEBA z-score features.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite. Primary keys are src_ip (v4/v6), dest_ip, host_id / asset_id (corporate asset inventory key), account_id / user_id (AD SID, UPN, Okta uid), domain (DNS), and ordered tuples (src_ip × dest_port), (src_ip × dest_ip), (src_ip × dest_ip × dest_port), (account_id × src_ip), (host_id × dest_host), (process × parent_process). Secondary keys ASN, geo, ja4 fingerprint, vlan/subnet/segment. The SOC also wants the dual asset/user view: a finding tied to host_id should be queryable as a feature of the assigned user, which is the UEBA 'entity' join.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate (60 s, 1m, 5m, 15m, 30m, 1h, 6h, 24h) to match the standard Cisco / Splunk / Elastic / Sigma detection-rule shapes. Tumbling 1m / 5m for compliance / reporting / SIEM downsampling. Session windows are useful for 'burst then quiet' beaconing and for grouping a lateral-movement chain across an interactive session. Approximate aggregates are mandatory at NetFlow / Zeek scale: HLL for n_unique(src_ip / dest_ip / dest_port / qname), CMS + Top-K for 'top scanners by distinct ports last 5 minutes', t-digest / DDSketch for inter-arrival-time distributions (beaconing), EWMA / Welford variance for UEBA z-scores. Exact counts are needed only when the counter feeds a compliance report.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once is acceptable across SIEM enrichment and detection — over-counting a failed-login event biases a velocity feature upward, which is the safe direction for security (fires alert slightly earlier). Idempotency on (event_id) is desirable for replay scenarios (SIEM re-ingest, agent retry) but not strictly required. The decision is a risk signal / alert, not a financial or regulated record, so beava's at-least-once posture matches the buyer's needs.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Read p99 <10 ms for inline / streaming enrichment (a SIEM ingestion pipeline that enriches every event with per-IP / per-asset features cannot tolerate a 100 ms lookup or it bottlenecks the whole ingest tier). Detection-rule evaluation tolerates 100 ms — 1 s. SOC analyst triage (clicking an alert to see enriched per-IP features) tolerates 1 — 5 s. SOAR enrichment playbooks tolerate seconds. beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits comfortably inside the streaming-enrichment budget, which is exactly the regime where a per-IP lookup against a remote Splunk lookup table or a cold S3 enrichment index is too slow.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to single-digit seconds. Modern detection guidance (Splunk Security Content, Elastic Security, Panther real-time rules) targets streaming evaluation rather than batch lookback, and a 30 — 120 s freshness lag (typical Splunk scheduled search cadence) is the gap beava can close. For an inline enrichment proxy in front of a SIEM ingest, freshness must be <1 s so the enriched event arrives in the SIEM with features computed from events that landed milliseconds earlier. For UEBA baselines (24 h / 7 d / 30 d), freshness can be minutes — but the hot rolling window for the active detection rule wants seconds.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state EPS for SIEM workloads is dominated by network and endpoint telemetry. A mid-size enterprise SOC ingests 1 — 10k EPS, a large bank 50 — 500k EPS, hyperscaler / telco / large-fed SOCs land at 1M+ EPS aggregate. Industry sizing rules of thumb: 1k EPS ≈ 86.4M events/day ≈ 8.6 GB/day; SIEM analyst staffing scales at roughly 1 analyst per 50 — 75 GB/day. A single beava node at the published ~684k EPS (M4, TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) covers a single large enterprise's combined network + auth telemetry (firewall + VPN + auth + DNS + proxy), but very large platforms must hand-shard by (src_ip / asset_id / tenant) prefix because beava v0 has no in-process sharding. CrowdStrike Falcon LogScale benchmarks at ~1 TB/node/day ingest (~12 — 120k EPS depending on event size); Splunk indexers are quoted at similar ranges. beava's value is not raw EPS — it is that the same EPS turns into queryable pre-aggregated per-entity features at sub-ms read, which Splunk / Sentinel achieve only via scheduled searches with their own freshness and cost penalties. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Roughly 1:1 to 1:3 read-to-write at the SIEM ingestion / enrichment tier (every flow / auth event is one write, and the enrichment shim issues 1 — 10 feature reads per event to compute the enriched record). The ratio tips toward read-heavy at the analyst / SOAR enrichment tier (one alert triggers tens to hundreds of feature reads for the related entities). Pure detection-rule evaluation is more write-skewed if rules are evaluated by polling beava counters.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by src_ip cardinality (Internet-facing) and host_id / account_id cardinality (corporate). A large enterprise sees ~50k — 500k internal asset IDs, ~50k — 500k corporate accounts, and the external-facing surface sees 1M — 10M+ distinct src_ip per day (with residential-proxy / botnet noise pushing the tail much higher). At ~500 B — 2 KB per per-entity feature row (a handful of sliding-window counters, an HLL sketch, a t-digest for beaconing inter-arrival, EWMA state), the hot keyspace is 1 — 20 GB for asset/account state plus 1 — 50 GB for src_ip state — fits in RAM on a single modern box for the corporate slice, but explosive on the external-IP slice during a DDoS or scan event without aggressive TTL/eviction. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Explosive on src_ip (especially external — millions of distinct /32s during scans or DDoS, billions across long retention), explosive on (src_ip × dest_ip × dest_port) tuples, slowly-growing on host_id / asset_id (~10k — 500k per enterprise), slowly-growing on account_id (similar order), bounded on dest_port (well-known ports cluster), bounded on protocol / vlan / asset_class. The cardinality blow-up on src_ip is the well-known reason SIEMs charge per GB and not per series, and the reason Splunk lookup tables / Sentinel watchlists rarely include 'all external IPs seen in last 7 days' as a queryable index.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Seconds to minutes for hot scan / brute-force / beacon-interval counters (the rolling 60 s — 15 m windows themselves plus a small late-arrival tail). 1 — 24 h for UEBA short-term baselines. 7 — 30 d for long-term IP / asset / user reputation that feeds risk scores (Splunk Asset & Identity, Sentinel watchlists, Chronicle entity context). Compliance retention (SOC 2, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP, NIS2) is 12 — 24 months or longer — but that lives in the SIEM's cold tier, not in beava; beava holds the hot pre-aggregated features and is allowed to forget once the SIEM has archived the raw event.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 5 — 30 features per inline enrichment (the standard 'per-IP rep + per-asset risk + per-user risk + per-(src_ip × dest_ip) flow stats' set). 20 — 100+ features per UEBA scoring decision (Splunk UEBA, Exabeam Smart Timelines, Securonix entity scores compute many per-entity behavioral features). 5 — 50 features per SOAR enrichment playbook step. Strongly favors batch_get — exactly what beava ships.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe. Hot rolling windows are derived state — losing 5 minutes of per-IP scan counters during a node restart degrades detection briefly (windows refill) but does not produce a regulatory error because the raw events still live in the SIEM cold tier and can be re-replayed. The compliance / regulator-grade record lives in the SIEM (Splunk indexers, Sentinel Log Analytics, S3-archived raw events) — beava is not the system-of-record for SOC 2 / PCI-DSS / HIPAA / FedRAMP / NIS2 audit logs. beava's WAL + snapshot is sufficient for the hot tier; some buyers will accept WAL-disabled for higher EPS, because the cost of losing a window is bounded.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for a per-VPC / per-segment / per-region sidecar topology, co-located with the SIEM forwarder (Splunk Universal Forwarder, Elastic Agent, Sentinel Agent, Cribl Stream worker, Bindplane / OTel collector). Sidecar-next-to-NetFlow-collector or sidecar-next-to-Zeek is the natural shape; beava holds the rolling features local to where the flow data is decoded, and the enriched record is forwarded to the SIEM cold tier. Multi-region active-active is rarely required because most rules are region-local (a port scan on the EU edge is decided in the EU). The hard limit is no in-process sharding in v0 — a single tenant beyond ~684k EPS or tens of GB of hot src_ip state must hand-shard externally (e.g., by /16 prefix or asset_id prefix). beava's 'refuse-on-network-FS' restriction is fine because SOC sidecars universally co-locate state with the process.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Detection-engineering / SOC platform engineering / SecOps platform teams at: (a) large enterprises running Splunk Enterprise Security, Microsoft Sentinel, Google SecOps (Chronicle), Elastic Security, Sumo Logic Cloud SIEM or Datadog Cloud SIEM and hitting per-GB ingest cost ceilings or per-tenant search-latency ceilings on high-cardinality enrichment lookups; (b) MSSPs / MDR vendors (Arctic Wolf, eSentire, Expel, Red Canary, Critical Start, Trustwave) building per-customer enrichment pipelines feeding a multi-tenant SIEM; (c) cloud-native SIEM vendors (Panther, Anvilogic, Hunters, Devo, Securonix) building detection-as-code platforms that need a hot pre-aggregation tier; (d) NDR / XDR vendors (Vectra, Darktrace, ExtraHop, Corelight, CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne) embedding per-asset rolling features into their own scoring; (e) SOC2 / FedRAMP / HIPAA / PCI-DSS / NIS2 compliance teams who need real-time correlation across high-cardinality entity surfaces without exploding the SIEM bill. The buyer is detection engineering / SecOps platform — NOT the SOC analyst (who reads alerts in the SIEM UI) and NOT the security architect (who picks the SIEM). The persona is closest to platform / SRE at fraud / observability sibling use cases (#14).
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: SIEM market itself is ~$12 B in 2026 growing to ~$20 B by 2031 at ~11.5% CAGR (Mordor Intelligence) — top 5 vendors control ~55% of revenue. Microsoft Sentinel grew workloads 150% YoY in 2025; Cisco closed the $28 B Splunk acquisition March 2024; Google Chronicle integrated Gemini LLM in 2025; CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM (LogScale/Humio) generates $585M+ ARR. UEBA software is a parallel ~$1.3 B in 2024 growing to ~$19 B by 2032 at ~40% CAGR (Verified Market Research; analyst estimates diverge widely so the 2032 number is aggressive). NDR is its own ~$3 — 5 B segment (Vectra, Darktrace, ExtraHop, Corelight named Leaders in the May 2025 Gartner Magic Quadrant for NDR). beava's serviceable slice is not the full SIEM TAM — it is the 'pre-aggregation / enrichment / hot rolling-features' tier between event ingest and detection rules, which is the slice Cribl ($1B+ valuation), Bindplane, Databahn, Mezmo, Edge Delta and similar telemetry-pipeline vendors are monetizing today. SIEM ingest pricing (Splunk ES $250 — $400/GB/day list, Sentinel $5.22/GB pay-as-you-go) is the public proxy for the pain that pre-aggregation relieves. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) SIEM per-GB ingest cost is the dominant SOC budget pressure — pre-aggregating high-cardinality per-IP / per-asset rolling features outside the SIEM and ingesting only enriched alerts directly addresses this. 2) NIS2 (in force October 2024 across the EU) explicitly requires essential entities to use a tool for continuous evaluation of detected cybersecurity events and to correlate information in real time — drives broader real-time detection investment. 3) DORA (in force January 2025) puts operational-resilience pressure on EU financial-sector SOCs. 4) FedRAMP High and CMMC 2.0 mature requirements drive federal contractor spend on real-time SIEM monitoring. 5) Alert fatigue is a top-3 SOC pain — 'cardinality-threshold' rule patterns (n_unique > X in window Y) are the standard remedy and exactly what beava primitives express. 6) Detection-as-Code adoption (Panther pypanther, Anvilogic, Splunk Security Content as code, Elastic Detection Rules in GitHub, Sigma rule ecosystem at >3000 rules) drives demand for a Python-native feature store the rules can read from — beava's @bv.event / @bv.table fits the same author experience. 7) Move from EDR → XDR → NDR / NDR-bundled-with-SIEM consolidation (CrowdStrike Falcon LogScale, Microsoft Sentinel + Defender XDR, Google SecOps unification) creates platform-engineering teams who own the pre-aggregation tier as a discrete component.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: SOC 2 Type II (auditable retention, access logging, monitoring — universal for SaaS / MSSP / SIEM vendor stacks). PCI-DSS v4.0 (12 months log retention, real-time alerting on high-risk events, file-integrity monitoring) — beava v0's lack of TLS / auth is a hard blocker for PCI scope. HIPAA security rule (PHI access logging, retention 6 years) — same TLS / auth blocker. FedRAMP Moderate / High (NIST 800-53 control families — AU, SI, IR; continuous-monitoring requirements; FIPS-140 crypto) — beava v0 cannot deploy into a FedRAMP boundary without FIPS-validated TLS and authenticated access. NIS2 (continuous monitoring + incident reporting within 24/72 hours for EU 'essential entities'). CMMC 2.0 / DFARS for US defense contractors. GDPR / CCPA on IP-as-PII (short-TTL / hashing helps — beava's in-memory TTL story is friendly here, but lack of auth is still a blocker). Note beava is NOT the system-of-record for these regulators — the SIEM cold tier is — so beava's compliance scope is limited to 'transit and access controls of the pre-aggregation tier', which is still substantial.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast for the demo: 1 — 3 days to a working 'per-source-IP failed-login counter + n_unique(account_id) password-spray detector + n_unique(dest_port) port-scan detector + impossible-travel distance' demo on a laptop using @bv.event / @bv.table primitives plus a thin Sigma-rule evaluator that calls batch_get. 2 — 6 weeks to a production pilot at an MSSP / mid-enterprise SOC, gated mainly by TLS / auth (v0 gap below) and by wiring up SIEM-side ingestion of the enriched records (Cribl Stream, OTel-collector, or a direct Splunk HEC shim). Production at a FedRAMP-bounded customer or PCI-scope deployment is materially longer (6 — 18 months) and gated on the FIPS / TLS / auth engineering.

competition.incumbents: Generic real-time stack: Redis + Lua sliding-window counters (the overwhelming default for SOC enrichment lookups), Elasticsearch enrich processor + watchlists (Splunk / Elastic / Sentinel lookup tables), Apache Flink stateful streaming for SIEM optimization (Confluent publishes Flink-as-SIEM-front-end patterns), Apache Kafka + ksqlDB / Materialize / RisingWave for the SIEM pre-aggregation tier. Telemetry-pipeline incumbents: Cribl Stream, Bindplane / Google's OTel-collector commercial, Databahn, Mezmo, Edge Delta, Tenzir — these vendors monetize 'route, filter, aggregate before the SIEM' and frequently bundle a key-value cache for enrichment but rarely a full feature-server. Stream-processing fabric: Confluent Cloud + Flink, AWS Kinesis Data Analytics, Apache Beam, Materialize. Cache / KV: Redis Enterprise (with Redis Bloom / CMS / Top-K), Aerospike, RonDB.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: For the per-IP / per-asset rolling-features-for-SOC slice specifically: Redis with Lua sliding-window scripts is the de-facto incumbent at almost every MSSP and mid-large SOC; bespoke in-Splunk lookup tables refreshed by scheduled searches (the Splunk Security Essentials / Enterprise Security Asset & Identity pattern) is the second-most-common. Cribl Stream's 'aggregations' processor is the named competitor for SIEM-cost-optimization pre-aggregation. Splunk UEBA, Exabeam Fusion / New-Scale, Securonix Next-Gen SIEM and Gurucul UEBA are vertically integrated UEBA platforms that compute these features internally and would not be displaced by beava — but the long tail of mid-enterprise SOCs that build their own detection engineering on Sigma + Panther + Elastic + Falcon LogScale + Wazuh genuinely lack a hot feature tier and currently make do with Redis + Lua. NDR vendors (Vectra Cognito, Darktrace, ExtraHop RevealX, Corelight) compute per-asset rolling features internally on appliances; beava could underlie a software NDR or extend an XDR vendor's per-asset signal set. Panther's pypanther (Python-native detection-as-code) is the closest cultural cousin and a likely natural integration target.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get for inline SIEM-ingest enrichment — Redis-with-Lua sliding-window counters typically land at 1 — 5 ms p99 and require custom Lua, while a remote Splunk lookup table or a scheduled search runs 100 ms — 10 s; beava's single-digit-microsecond reads are a structural fit. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives cover n_unique (HLL), velocity, distance, distribution (t-digest / DDSketch), inter-arrival-time variance (Welford / EWMA), and recency — i.e. exactly the primitives in Cisco / Splunk / Elastic / Sigma port-scan / brute-force / beaconing detection rules. The 'sliding HyperLogLog over destination ports per source IP' research finding maps to one beava @bv.table declaration. 3) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Redis-cluster — fits the per-VPC / per-segment sidecar shape and avoids the operational tax of running Flink + Kafka + ZooKeeper inside the SOC's airgapped or FedRAMP-bounded enclave. 4) Apache-2.0, no open-core, no SaaS-only — attractive to MSSPs and government SOCs that cannot ship customer data to a vendor cloud. 5) Push-on-event over HTTP / TCP+msgpack maps directly to OTel-collector and Cribl Stream patterns the SOC already runs. 6) Python-native author experience (@bv.event / @bv.table) is culturally aligned with detection-as-code (Panther pypanther, Anvilogic, Wazuh custom rules) — detection engineers can declare features in the same language as their rules. 7) The 'distance' primitive expresses impossible-travel as a single feature read instead of hand-rolled Haversine in a Splunk lookup or a Sentinel KQL function.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth in v0 — absolute disqualifier for any production SOC deployment, full stop. SOC traffic crosses trust boundaries by definition; PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP, NIS2 and SOC 2 all require encrypted-in-transit, authenticated and audit-logged access to security-relevant data. This is THE blocking gap for this domain, more so than for any other use case in the beava catalog. 2) No FIPS-140-validated crypto path — needed for FedRAMP High / DoD IL4-5 customers. 3) No multi-tenancy primitives — MSSPs serving many customers need per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant quotas, per-tenant audit logging on beava's own API surface. 4) No in-process sharding — a hyperscaler / telco / major-bank SOC at >684k EPS or tens of GB of hot src_ip state must hand-shard externally; Splunk indexers, Sentinel ingestion, Falcon LogScale (1 TB/node/day) and Elastic Security all shard internally. 5) No triggers / 'fire when feature crosses threshold' — detection rules want push-on-threshold semantics so the SIEM correlation engine doesn't have to poll thousands of (src_ip × feature) pairs. 6) No native SIEM connector / no documented Splunk HEC exporter, no Sentinel Log Analytics ingestion, no Chronicle UDM emitter, no Elastic ECS-conformant push — adoption blocker. 7) No PromQL / SPL / KQL query surface — SOC analysts use the SIEM UI for ad-hoc 'top 10 src_ips by distinct-port count last hour' and beava only serves features it has been told to compute (acceptable, but pushes beava into the pre-aggregation-tier role rather than 'replace my SIEM' framing). 8) No native Sigma rule import — buyers must rewrite Sigma rules as @bv.table declarations + a thin evaluator. 9) No documented MITRE ATT&CK technique → feature mapping in the repo today, which is the canonical detection-engineering taxonomy. 10) No long-horizon storage — 12 — 24 month log retention required by PCI / HIPAA / NIS2 / FedRAMP lives in the SIEM cold tier; beava is hot-tier-only.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: Zeek / Suricata / Snort NIDS (conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log push), NetFlow / sFlow / IPFIX collectors (nProbe, Akvorado, ntopng), VPC Flow Logs / AWS CloudTrail / Azure Activity Logs / GCP audit logs (via a Lambda / Function shim → HTTP push), Windows Event Forwarder / Sysmon (EID 4624 / 4625 / 4688), Linux auditd / journald, OpenVPN / WireGuard / Tailscale logs, EDR agents (CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender), proxy / WAF (Squid, Bluecoat, Cloudflare, F5), DNS resolvers (PowerDNS, BIND, Unbound, Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 for Teams). Telemetry-pipeline midstream: Cribl Stream → HTTP/TCP push, Bindplane / OTel-collector → exporter shim, Databahn, Tenzir, Vector.dev. Consumers: SIEM enrichment (Splunk HEC enrichment field, Sentinel custom log ingestion, Elastic enrich pipeline, Chronicle UDM, Sumo Logic Hosted Collector, Falcon LogScale HEC, Datadog Cloud SIEM, Panther log ingestion, Wazuh active-response), SOAR enrichment (Cortex XSOAR playbook step, Splunk SOAR, Tines, Torq, Swimlane), detection-rule evaluator (Sigma + sigmac, Panther pypanther, Anvilogic, in-house Drools / OPA), UEBA scorer (Splunk UEBA, Exabeam, Securonix, Gurucul — typically integrated, but extensible per-feature-API). beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 fits the Cribl / OTel-collector / Wazuh producer paths; TCP+msgpack :8081 fits the high-throughput NetFlow / Zeek path.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both, with most SOC weight on rules. Detection engineering is overwhelmingly rules-driven (Sigma + 3000+ open rules, Splunk Security Content, Elastic Detection Rules, Panther pypanther) reading beava features via batch_get. UEBA / risk-scoring is the ML side (entity-risk-score models in Splunk UEBA, Exabeam, Securonix, Gurucul, plus bespoke XGBoost / isolation-forest UEBA in-house) consuming the same beava rolling features. beava as a pure feature backend stays decoupled from both.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public beava users on this use case identified. [uncertain] Comparable production references and patterns at incumbents: Splunk publishes Enterprise Security UEBA reference architectures and Security Content detection library; Microsoft publishes Sentinel windowed Impossible Travel rule with concrete 500/1000/2000-mile × 2/4/6-hour thresholds; Okta documents the 500 mph travel-velocity behaviour; Cisco Secure Firewall publishes the 50-connections-30-seconds-different-ports port-scan correlation rule shape; Splunk Security Content publishes Internal Horizontal Port Scan detection; Elastic publishes a Statistical Model Detected C2 Beaconing prebuilt rule with sub-minute jitter analysis; Sigma main repository hosts 3000+ peer-reviewed detection rules including velocity-thresholded brute-force and port-scan rules; Panther publishes pypanther for Python-native real-time streaming detection. Springer Nature published 'Sliding HyperLogLog' for port-scan detection — academic reference for the exact feature shape beava would express. Confluent publishes Apache-Flink-as-SIEM-front-end reference architecture. Cribl publishes the Aggregate-data-in-Cribl-Stream-to-optimize-SIEM pattern. No vendor today positions beava-like 'sub-ms TCP+msgpack feature server, Apache-2.0, no broker' for this slice; that is the open positioning.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads located on this topic. [uncertain] Broader community signal is strong: r/cybersecurity and r/blueteamsec threads on SIEM cost optimization and pre-aggregation; r/sigma and SigmaHQ GitHub for detection-as-code discussion; Elastic detection-rules GitHub repo with active issue tracker; Splunk Security Content GitHub; Panther blog series on detection-as-code; Detection Engineering Weekly newsletter (Zack Allen); Detection at Scale blog (Jack Naglieri, Panther founder) including 'The New Economics of an AI-Powered SIEM'; Cribl community discussions on SIEM cost; multiple Hacker News threads on Splunk-vs-Sentinel-vs-LogScale pricing and on Cisco's Splunk acquisition. adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No dedicated SIEM / network-security / port-scan / brute-force / beaconing / impossible-travel demo identified in the repository. Existing demos cover adtech, ecommerce and fraud at /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/{adtech,ecommerce,fraud}. A purpose-built SIEM demo — auth_event + flow_event → per-source-IP failed-logins / failure-ratio / n_unique-account_id / n_unique-dest_port / inter-arrival-time-stddev / impossible-travel-distance, served via batch_get to a thin Sigma-style rule evaluator — would be a natural addition and would map directly onto MITRE T1110 / T1046 / T1071 / T1021 detection coverage. [uncertain]
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Maximum. SIEM detection is an actively adversarial domain — attackers explicitly tune brute-force / password-spray cadence to stay below threshold (low-and-slow), randomize C2 beacon intervals to defeat jitter analysis, rotate residential-proxy IPs to defeat per-IP velocity, and stage lateral movement to live below per-asset baselines. Feature drift is fast; detection engineers add and retire features continuously, which argues for a developer-ergonomic feature backend (beava's Python-native @bv.event / @bv.table) rather than a SQL-on-Flink pipeline or a Lua-on-Redis script library. The adversary pressure here is comparable to fraud / bot defence (use cases 1a — 4) and materially higher than observability (#14).

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Replacing the SIEM — beava is not the system-of-record for security events; raw events, compliance retention (12 — 24 months PCI / HIPAA / NIS2 / FedRAMP), forensic replay, ad-hoc SPL/KQL search, and the analyst UI all stay in Splunk / Sentinel / Chronicle / Elastic / Falcon LogScale. 2) Replacing the NDR / XDR — Vectra, Darktrace, ExtraHop, Corelight, CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne own the appliance / agent + ML + UI stack; beava sits underneath one of them at most. 3) Long-horizon historical correlation / threat-hunting lookback (>30 — 90 d) — beava is in-memory only; the cold archive lives elsewhere. 4) Cross-entity joins ('show me all assets that ever talked to this C2 IP and shared a parent process') — beava has no join engine; that is graph-DB (Apache TinkerPop, Neo4j) or OLAP (ClickHouse, Druid) territory. 5) Acting as the SIEM correlation engine — beava feeds the rule, it is not the rule evaluator. 6) Acting as the alert UI / case management — Splunk ES Mission Control, Sentinel Investigation Graph, Chronicle SOAR, IBM QRadar, Panther / TheHive / Tines own this. 7) Acting as the threat-intel store — MISP, ThreatConnect, Anomali, Recorded Future, Mandiant Advantage own that surface; beava can hold per-IP risk features but is not a TIP. 8) Compliance source-of-truth (PCI / HIPAA / FedRAMP / NIS2 audit logs) — that obligation lives in the SIEM cold tier.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for SIEM enrichment, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination, mutual TLS, and a tokened / mTLS auth model on :8080, :8081 and :8090 — absolute precondition, no production SOC ships without it. 2) FIPS-140-validated crypto path — gates FedRAMP Moderate / High, DoD IL4 — IL5, and most US federal contractor SOCs. 3) Audit logging of every admin and push API call (who, when, what was written / read) — required for SOC 2 Type II, PCI-DSS 10, HIPAA security rule, FedRAMP AU control family, NIS2. 4) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant quotas, per-tenant audit logs, per-tenant rate-limit accounting — MSSPs serving many customers cannot deploy beava without this. 5) Native Splunk HEC / Sentinel Log Analytics / Chronicle UDM / Elastic ECS / Falcon LogScale HEC / OpenTelemetry-collector exporters — adoption blocker, every other observability/security backend ships these. 6) Native Sigma rule import (sigmac-style translator) so detection engineers can express their existing rule library as @bv.table declarations + a thin evaluator with minimal rewrites. 7) Triggers / 'fire when feature crosses threshold' — detection rules are inherently event-driven; polling 100k (src_ip × feature) pairs every 10 s is wasteful and one round-trip slower than a callback. 8) HLL / CMS / Top-K / Bloom / t-digest / DDSketch / Welford-EWMA documented as first-class aggregations and exhaustively benchmarked — the 50+ primitives must explicitly cover n_unique(dest_port) for port-scan, n_unique(account_id) for password-spray, inter-arrival-time distribution for beaconing, and EWMA z-score for UEBA. 9) Per-entity TTL / sliding-window eviction with a documented memory budget — src_ip cardinality is unbounded in the worst case (DDoS / scan storms), and the buyer needs a 'set max RAM, evict-by-TTL-then-LRU' guarantee. 10) IP / ASN / GeoIP enrichment hooks (either as in-process modules or as a documented producer pattern with MaxMind GeoLite2 / Team Cymru / similar). 11) MITRE ATT&CK technique → feature catalogue in docs (T1110 brute-force, T1046 port-scan, T1071 C2 beaconing, T1021 lateral movement, T1078 valid accounts impossible-travel) showing the canonical @bv.event / @bv.table for each. 12) In-process or sidecar sharding by (src_ip prefix / asset_id / tenant) so a hyperscaler / telco / major-bank SOC can scale within one cluster without hand-sharding. 13) A Cribl Stream destination plugin and a Bindplane / OTel-collector exporter so beava sits transparently in existing SOC telemetry pipelines. 14) Cold-start strategy: WAL replay time on a node with tens of GB of hot src_ip state must be benchmarked and bounded; otherwise a node restart becomes an outage during an active scan / DDoS. 15) GDPR / CCPA tombstone-by-account_id / by-src_ip primitive — IPs are PII in the EU, and the SOC must be able to honour erasure requests on hot features.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — strongly preferred. Detection rules are inherently event-driven: 'fire when src_ip.distinct_dest_ports_60s > 20 (Cisco port-scan threshold)', 'fire when account_id.failure_count_5m > 5 AND success_count_immediately_after > 0 (brute-force-then-success)', 'fire when (src_ip × dest_ip × dest_port).interarrival_stddev < 2s for last 10 events (beacon)'. The natural shape is a push-on-threshold callback into the SIEM ingest / SOAR / rule evaluator, not a poll-every-N-seconds loop over feature keys. Pure analyst / SOAR enrichment slices (looking up features on demand for an alert) need only feature serving, no triggers.
